title: Family background; wagon trip to Idaho; parents and siblings
description: Myrtle Bening provides her name and birth details and recalls her family's journey by uncovered wagon from Farmington, Washington to Bonners Ferry, Idaho in 1893. She names her parents, Mary Haptonstall and William Wilson Johnson, and describes her father's move from farming to running a meat market. She also names her older sisters and brothers, and explains her sister Nora's married name change from Stingist to Stonechest.

title: Bonners Ferry flood; Troy; railroad work and early mining
description: Myrtle recounts how a sudden flood forced the family to charter a train and relocate to Troy, where they occupied an empty hotel. She describes an incident with a pet bear belonging to saloon keeper Ed Riley. She discusses the economic landscape of early Troy, including railroad tie-cutting for the Great Northern, prospecting for lead at the Old Snowstorm mill, and subsistence hunting.

title: Husband's ranger career; trapping and logging
description: She describes her husband Frank Fedile's early career, including his Forest Service training at the University of Montana in Missoula for five dollars a week. She recounts his move to Green Bay and his partnership with an old trapper before becoming a ranger. She notes that he quit the ranger service because of her poor health and isolation, turning to logging instead.

title: Children; son's timber business
description: Myrtle names her two sons, Fred and Jem, and their birth years during the 1910 fire and 1913. She details her younger son's successful timber business in Bonners Ferry, which included a sawmill, a treating plant, and his own chemical solution for mahogany, before his recent serious illness and surgery.

title: Cooking for loggers; wartime work; husband's origins
description: Myrtle recalls her work cooking through the war for lumberjacks and explains how Frank came from Green Bay, Wisconsin to the West. She describes his success logging with oxen in steep, brushy country alongside her brother-in-law.

title: The 1910 fire; childbirth experiences
description: She recounts the 1910 big fire, describing the drought, her hospitalization for a breast infection, and her escape on foot from the ranger station with her newborn as the fire approached Wallace. She then explains that both sons were born at home without a doctor for Fred's arrival and with a traveling retired doctor for Jem's twelve-pound birth.

title: Education; cooking skills; nursing home life
description: Myrtle states she had two years of high school before having to work. She lists cooking as her primary skill and passion, and describes selling her three rental properties and home to move to the Shoshone Convalescent Inn. She mentions her plan to fly to Vancouver from Spokane to visit a niece and notes her great-grandsons' military service.

title: Cooking camps; nursing work; hobbies and lodge
description: She describes her work cooking for logging crews and informally helping with nursing in earlier years. She shares how she loved reading, knitting, and playing piano before her eyesight failed, and explains her fifty-year membership in the Eastern Star, the women's organization of the Masons.

title: The 1916 flood; recovery; Depression
description: Myrtle recounts the devastating 1916 flood that forced her to flee rising waters by climbing out a window with her children. She describes the loss of her home and supplies, including a quarter of beef filled with gravel and a case of butter, and the slow recovery made possible by fruit from friends. She contrasts this with the Depression years when her husband held a steady timber chief job that allowed them to help hungry neighbors.

title: Frugal cooking; modern domestic skills
description: Myrtle Bening describes her 'Bean Loaf' recipe made from ground beans, cheap meat, and spices, and she and Connie Richard discuss how modern families lack basic cooking and sewing skills compared to previous generations.

title: First phonograph; early movies and TV
description: Myrtle Bening recalls her first phonograph experience at her mother's hotel where she lost a nickel to an inappropriate song, her first silent motion picture in Libby, and seeing her first television at a Green Bay tavern.

title: Husband's character; family life
description: Myrtle Bening describes her late husband as a quiet, honest, well-liked man from a Green Bay logging family who left the Catholic Church, never spanked their children, and died at 72; she explains her husband's belief that there was no such thing as a bad child.

title: Elderly finances; healthcare costs
description: Myrtle Bening discusses the financial struggles of nursing home residents on Social Security, high medication costs, and the facility's refusal to accept Medicaid, while also explaining her own failing eyesight prevents reading and writing.

title: Working mothers; daycare debate
description: Myrtle Bening argues that mothers should stay home with children rather than work and use daycare, criticizing babysitters and asserting that a mother's love is irreplaceable.

title: Welfare criticism
description: Myrtle Bening expresses disapproval of welfare dependency, recounting her experience as a landlord to a welfare recipient who misbehaved and couldn't be evicted due to government intervention.

title: Changing family dynamics; elder care
description: Myrtle Bening observes that modern women have different social lives, recounts caring for five elderly family members herself, and explains her decision to live in a nursing home rather than burden her children.

title: Childhood holidays; courtship
description: Myrtle Bening shares memories of her first Christmas on the Farmington farm, describes the dresses she wore when meeting her husband, and recounts their courtship involving dances and shows without chaperones.

title: Neighbor's tragedy
description: Myrtle Bening tells the story of a neighboring woman in Reno whose son was killed in a hunting accident by his stepfather, causing the mother to lose her mind and die from grief.

title: Daily routine; marriage
description: Myrtle Bening describes her early married life on five dollars a week, her daily cooking routine, and how she met her husband when he worked for her brother-in-law.

title: Pioneer migration; father
description: Myrtle Bening recounts her family's journey by covered wagon from Missouri to Oregon and Washington, her father's origin as an abandoned English infant, and his role as Whitman County's first commissioner.

title: Social life; dancing
description: Myrtle Bening recalls never missing a dance in her youth when alcohol was absent, singing in the church choir, and contrasts this with modern drinking culture.

title: Meeting husband; courtship details
description: Myrtle Bening explains how she met her husband, their chaperone-free courtship, her first kiss from the preacher's son, and marrying at 22 after being considered an old maid.

title: Family history; welfare story
description: Myrtle Bening discusses her brother's birth as possibly the first white child in Whitman County and tells a story about raising the rent on a welfare tenant.

title: Native American relations; Chief Joseph
description: Myrtle Bening describes the railroad agreement with Native Americans and recounts the community's evacuation to Colfax during Chief Joseph's war-path scare when she was a baby.

title: Closing remarks
description: Myrtle Bening concludes the interview asking if she has been helpful.
